debate_title: Should frontier AI development be gated by compute-thresh...

conflicts.point: What signal should screen a model into the pre-deployment behavioral hold for irreversible capabilities — a pre-weights signal observable mid-training (compute or a statutory capability-trigger list), or only post-training behavioral evaluation once weights exist.

positions.stance: An irreversible capability cannot be screened only after weights exist, because weights mirrored across machines cannot be recalled; a pre-weights screen (compute observability plus an enumerated capability-trigger list) is required to route suspect runs into the behavioral hold before the artifact is loose.

A behavioral checkpoint on a short enumerated hazard list suffices; a compute or input-side screen sweeps in the entire frontier and licenses the foundry rather than locking the specific dangerous capability.

A compute signal is only observable as a single dense event for the honest single-site, single-run, reporting builder; a determined developer distills, splits across jurisdictions and months, and assembles frontier capability so no single run crosses the line, so the tripwire screens the wrong actor.

conflicts.point: Whether distributing halt/veto authority across multiple bodies reduces capture risk or merely multiplies the points of lobbying and definitional rent-seeking.

positions.stance: Distributing halt authority with asymmetric resumption (one body can veto, resuming requires concurrence across the set) makes the regime fail toward caution; capture of one node cannot force deployment, only capture of every node can, and a statutory capability list makes threshold changes visible contestable acts.

Every added node is another comment docket, definitional margin, and re-authorization markup; historically FCC spectrum, bank charters, and FAA certification show more interlocutors meant more doors for incumbent lawyers, and rent-seeking lives in scope-language and boundary interpretation, not the headline number.

Distributing veto authority multiplies the offices an incumbent must lobby and the sunset clock converts the moat into a recurring lobbying event; quietly nudging a FLOP threshold in a markup is invisible while adding a hazard to a statute is visible and contestable.

conflicts.point: Whether the converged regime's institutional capacity and budget will actually fund the everyday-harm reporting layer and the public evaluation body, or will be consumed by the catastrophic-tail gate.

positions.stance: The tail-gate and the everyday-harm reporting standard are different layers and a regime can build both, with publicly-funded evaluation capacity so small developers are not priced out.

No one has named who pays for the public evaluation capacity or its headcount, and the everyday-harm reporting layer risks being eaten by the prestige tail-gate, the way aviation incident-reporting took decades and a body count to fund.

verdicts.conflict: What signal should route a model into the pre-deployment behavioral hold: a pre-weights signal (compute plus a capability-trigger list) or only post-training behavioral evaluation.
verdicts.rationale: C19 establishes a valid logical point that behavioral evaluation cannot fire before weights exist, so an irreversible artifact can escape any post-hoc screen; C20 and C22 supply an equally valid counterpoint that a compute trigger captures the honest single-run builder while a determined developer distills and splits runs across jurisdictions to stay under any line. Both rest on contested empirical predictions about evasion behavior and recall feasibility that neither side substantiates with data. The disagreement reduces to which failure mode is more frequent, which the existing record does not yet settle.
verdicts.whatWouldChange: Empirical evidence on how often frontier capability is reached through split or distilled training runs that evade a single-run compute threshold, versus how often dangerous weights propagate irreversibly after release, would tip the balance.

verdicts.conflict: Whether distributing halt and resumption authority across multiple bodies reduces capture risk or multiplies lobbying and rent-seeking entry points.
verdicts.rationale: C24 cites three concrete licensing precedents — FCC spectrum, national bank charters, FAA type certification — and challenges the opposing side to name a multi-node regime where distributed authority demonstrably resisted capture better than a single regulator, an unanswered demand in the map. C23's asymmetric-resumption design is logically coherent and specifies a fail-toward-caution mechanism, but it rests on an untested institutional prediction rather than documented cases. C24 also identifies that rent-seeking operates through scope-language and boundary interpretation rather than node count, a more specific causal account.
verdicts.whatWouldChange: A documented case of a multi-body regulatory regime with asymmetric resumption authority that resisted incumbent capture better than a comparable single-regulator regime would shift the verdict toward C23.

verdicts.conflict: Whether a converged regime will actually fund the everyday-harm reporting layer and public evaluation body, or whether the catastrophic-tail gate will consume the budget.
verdicts.rationale: C25 names a concrete historical pattern — aviation incident-reporting took decades and accumulated fatalities before it was funded — and identifies the unanswered question of who pays for evaluation headcount. C16 asserts that a regime can build both layers and fund public evaluation capacity, but supplies no funding source, headcount estimate, or precedent for the two layers coexisting. On specificity and evidence C25 is more concrete; C16 states a possibility without demonstrating it.
verdicts.whatWouldChange: A funded budget line, headcount commitment, or an existing regime where a tail-risk gate and a diffuse-harm reporting layer were resourced simultaneously would strengthen C16.

verdicts.conflict: Whether a compute-threshold license functions as an anti-concentration tool or as a moat entrenching incumbents.
verdicts.rationale: C5 and C9 cite the structural regressivity of a fixed compliance cost and a consistent licensing-capture pattern across spectrum, banking, and aviation. C14 and C15 respond with design features — statutory sunset, distributed halt authority, capability-indexed thresholds exempting sub-frontier releases — that are specific and testable but remain proposals without operating precedent. The capture prediction draws on documented regulatory history while the mitigation rests on untested design.
verdicts.whatWouldChange: Evidence that capability-indexed thresholds with sunsets have kept compliance costs off small developers in an analogous licensing regime would shift weight toward C14 and C15.

verdicts.conflict: Whether regulators should gate on the size of the training input or only on demonstrated behavior at the point of use.
verdicts.rationale: C8 correctly observes that finance, aviation, and pharma test the product rather than the input, but C13 reframes the compute threshold as a tripwire that determines when to test rather than a safety verdict, citing the EU AI Act's 10^25 FLOP systemic classification that triggers risk assessment rather than declaring safety. This distinction defuses the analogy without denying it, since a test-routing trigger and a behavioral verdict are not mutually exclusive. C20's rebuttal that a hold need not become a foundry license remains, but the narrow logical claim in C13 survives the analogy attack.
verdicts.whatWouldChange: Evidence that compute correlates so weakly with hazardous capability that it mis-routes most cases would undermine C13's tripwire framing and favor C8's behavior-only position.

verdicts.conflict: Whether upstream developer liability for downstream harm kills open-source release or can be bounded by a safe harbor.
verdicts.rationale: C11 makes the valid point that joint-and-several liability for every downstream modification deters weight release, and notes negligence doctrine already severs causation when a downstream actor materially alters a system. C17 offers a more specific mechanism — a compliant-release safe harbor conditioned on provenance metadata and independent pre-release evaluation that protects against strict liability for third-party misuse — which directly addresses the deterrence problem with testable conditions. C17's concreteness on the conditions for protection gives it the edge.
verdicts.whatWouldChange: Evidence that safe-harbor conditions still impose prohibitive cost or legal uncertainty on small open-weight teams would restore C11's force.

verdicts.conflict: Whether experience-rated insurance can substitute for an ex-ante pre-deployment hold.
verdicts.rationale: C12, conceded by the same camp that advances C10, acknowledges that insurance misses diffuse small-dollar harm and cannot price catastrophic-tail damage exceeding developer solvency. C19 then validly identifies the point where the price signal dies as the point an ex-ante hold is needed. The concession in C12 leaves insurance positioned as a complement rather than a substitute, which C19 exploits without logical gap.
verdicts.whatWouldChange: A mechanism showing insurance markets can price or pool unrecoverable catastrophic-tail risk — analogous to Price-Anderson nuclear pooling — would weaken the case for a separate ex-ante hold.
